blocks.explanation:
A proof about an endless product. Every base is a power of 2, so the product is 2 raised to the sum of the powers.
That sum of powers is an infinite A.G.P.
Plan: write bases as powers of 2, combine into \(2^S\), find \(S\) by multiply-by-\(r\)-and-subtract, then work out \(2^S\).
steps:
Given: \(2^{\frac12} \cdot 4^{\frac14} \cdot 8^{\frac18} \cdot 16^{\frac{1}{16}} \cdots\)
To find: show that the product equals 4.
Method: Laws of indices \((x^m)^k = x^{mk}\), \(x^m x^k = x^{m+k}\), then the A.G.P. method for the sum of the powers.

Write every base as a power of 2
\[4 = 2^{2},\ 8 = 2^{3},\ 16 = 2^{4}\]
\[\text{L.H.S.} = 2^{\frac12} (2^{2})^{\frac14}\]
\[\quad \times (2^{3})^{\frac18} (2^{4})^{\frac{1}{16}} \cdots\]
Why: With one common base the powers can be combined.

Combine into one power of 2
\[= 2^{\frac12} \cdot 2^{\frac24} \cdot 2^{\frac38} \cdot 2^{\frac{4}{16}} \cdots\]
\[= 2^{\frac12 + \frac24 + \frac38 + \frac{4}{16} + \cdots}\]
\[= 2^{S}\]
Why: A power of a power multiplies: \((2^2)^{\frac14} = 2^{\frac24}\); same base multiplied: add the powers.

Sum the powers (an infinite A.G.P.)
\[S = \dfrac{1}{2} + \dfrac{2}{4} + \dfrac{3}{8} + \dfrac{4}{16} + \cdots\]
\[\tfrac{1}{2}S = \dfrac{1}{4} + \dfrac{2}{8} + \dfrac{3}{16} + \cdots\]
\[\tfrac{1}{2}S = \dfrac{1}{2} + \dfrac{1}{4} + \dfrac{1}{8} + \cdots\]
\[= \dfrac{\frac{1}{2}}{1 - \frac{1}{2}} = 1\]
\[S = 2\]
Why: The powers \(\frac{1}{2}, \frac{2}{4}, \frac{3}{8}, \ldots\) have tops \(1, 2, 3, \ldots\) (A.P.) and bottoms \(2, 4, 8, \ldots\) (G.P., \(r = \frac12\)). Multiply by \(\frac12\), shift and subtract; each pair leaves 1 on top. The result is an infinite G.P. with first term \(\frac12\), ratio \(\frac12\), sum 1; so \(S = 2\).

Work out the product
\[\text{L.H.S.} = 2^{S} = 2^{2} = 4 = \text{R.H.S.}\]
Why: Put \(S = 2\).
